rewrites.reskin: Accurate estimation of epidemic transmission dynamics is critical for enhancing public health response, resource allocation, and outbreak containment. With the increasing integration of heterogeneous surveillance sources such as wastewater monitoring, hospital admissions, and genomic sampling, the knowledge of disease spread dynamics has become more necessary than ever for timely intervention and policy control. Although recent advances in digital reporting infrastructure have reduced latency and transcription error significantly, these surveillance signals remain corrupted by observation noise and reporting delays. Therefore, noisy incidence measurements must be filtered to recover accurate transmission dynamics. In this work, compartmental epidemic state variables -- including effective reproduction number, latent population, and recovered fraction -- are estimated using extended Kalman filter (EKF) and unscented Kalman filter (UKF) applied to nonlinear SEIR dynamics. Case studies are performed on the 2009 H1N1 influenza outbreak in two U.S. census regions and the 2020 COVID-19 wave across three European countries. Results show that UKF and EKF can accurately track epidemic dynamics, with comparative performance reported across both scenarios.
rewrites.math: Accurate estimation of power system dynamics is critical for enhancing reliability, resilience, security, and stability of power systems. With increasing integration of inverter-based distributed energy resources, knowledge of dynamic states has become more necessary than ever for proper control and operation. Although recent advances in measurement devices have reduced transmission error significantly, measurements remain corrupted by observation noise. Therefore, noisy measurements must be processed to recover accurate operating dynamics. In this work, power system dynamic states are estimated using a particle filter (PF) and an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF), both of which represent the posterior state distribution through a finite ensemble of samples rather than propagating a Gaussian approximation through a linearized or sigma-point transform. Case studies are performed on the WECC 3-machine 9-bus system and the New England 10-machine 39-bus benchmark. Results show that ensemble-based methods accurately estimate power system dynamics. Comparative performance of PF and EnKF for the tested cases, including computational cost at varying ensemble sizes, is also provided.

rewrites.reskin:
Speaker localization in reverberant rooms: A Gaussian mixture model approach to microphone array misalignment

Context. Measurements of acoustic intensity and beamforming profiles from distributed microphone arrays typically rely on an assumed source location, which is taken to be the dominant energy peak or other proxies for the true acoustic emitter position. Departure of the assumed source position from the true emitter location biases the resultant directional profile measurements, an effect known as array misalignment bias. Aims. Currently, misalignment is typically modeled in stacked recordings from multiple sessions using a two-parameter model. We use an alternate approach in which the profiles of individual recordings are used with the corresponding likelihood computed using a Gaussian mixture model. Methods. We test the approach using simulated room impulse responses and corresponding beamformed spatial profiles from the OpenRIR synthetic reverberation dataset. Results. We obtain significantly improved estimates of the misalignment parameters for both 3D free-field and projected 2D far-field configurations relevant for real-world deployment. We discuss applications to upcoming large-scale acoustic sensing arrays.
rewrites.math:
Galaxy cluster profiles: A variational Bayes approach to halo miscentering

Context. Measurements of the galaxy density and weak-lensing profiles of galaxy clusters typically rely on an assumed cluster center, which is taken to be the brightest cluster galaxy or other proxies for the true halo center. Departure of the assumed cluster center from the true halo center biases the resultant profile measurements, an effect known as miscentering bias. Aims. Currently, miscentering is typically modeled in stacked profiles of clusters with a two-parameter model. We use an alternate approach in which the profiles of individual clusters are used with the corresponding posterior approximated via a mean-field variational Bayes factorization over a Student-t mixture prior, optimizing the evidence lower bound rather than evaluating a closed-form mixture likelihood. Methods. We test the approach using halos and the corresponding subhalo profiles from the IllustrisTNG hydrodynamic simulations. Results. We obtain significantly improved estimates of the miscentering parameters for both 3D and projected 2D profiles relevant for imaging surveys. We discuss applications to upcoming cosmological surveys.

rewrites.reskin:
Supply-chain centrality reveals the tendency of indirect transactions to homogenize the functional importance of firms in production networks

Economists and industrial strategists need to identify the relative importance of firms to make sound policy decisions and effectively allocate scarce intervention resources. We introduce a new method, termed supply-chain centrality, to determine the relative importance of a firm in a production network with respect to economy-wide monetary-material exchange. We demonstrate the uniqueness of supply-chain centrality by comparing it to other common centrality metrics and then show its economic significance. Specifically, we tested two hypotheses on a set of 50 empirically-based inter-firm transaction network models. The first concerned the distribution of centrality across the economy. We hypothesized that the functional importance of firms would tend to be concentrated into a few dominant suppliers followed by a group of firms with lower, more even importance. Second, we tested the hypothesis that indirect transactions homogenize the functional importance of firms. Our results support both hypotheses and highlight the importance of intermediaries and logistics providers in generating monetary-material flow. A core contribution is a formal mathematical method quantifying firm importance by integrating direct, indirect, and boundary transaction effects.
rewrites.math:
Spectral decomposition of trophic interaction matrices reveals dominant modes of energy transfer and species influence in ecosystems

Ecologists and conservation biologists need to identify the relative importance of species to make sound management decisions and effectively allocate scarce resources. We introduce a new method, termed spectral species ranking, to determine the relative importance of a species in an ecosystem network by computing a non-negative matrix factorization of the empirical trophic interaction matrix. Rather than aggregating flow along paths, we decompose the interaction matrix into a small set of latent trophic modes; the loading of each species onto the principal mode serves as its importance score. We demonstrate the uniqueness of spectral species ranking by comparing it to other common importance metrics and then show its ecological significance. Specifically, we tested two hypotheses on a set of 50 empirically-based ecosystem network models. Our results reveal that the leading spectral component captures a diffuse, broadly shared trophic role, with importance scores that cluster more tightly than dominance-diversity curves predict. Our findings highlight the role of detritus and nutrient recyclers and suggest that low-rank trophic structure underpins species substitutability in ecosystems.

rewrites.reskin: Context. Next-generation electroencephalography (EEG) recording systems targeting clinical seizure detection are increasingly deployed on awake, ambulatory patients, yielding high-cadence, high signal-to-noise neural traces. Because these recordings are sensitive to structured brain rhythms -- alpha oscillations, slow cortical potentials, and muscular artifacts -- even in neurotypical subjects, they are fundamentally limited by physiological background variability. Robust methods to account for and correct such variability are therefore essential. Aims. We evaluated the performance of Gaussian process (GP) regression for characterising brief ictal events embedded in continuous EEG, and in particular to determine how many variability components are necessary to describe wideband, high-cadence traces expected from next-generation amplifiers. Methods. We modelled background neural variability using GPs with different combinations of oscillatory, slow-drift, and artefact components, performing Bayesian model comparison to identify the optimal activity model. We compared the best multi-component model against the standard one-component GP and a non-GP baseline. Results. The best model contained four to five components -- one alpha-band oscillation, two to four slow-drift components, and one muscular modulation term -- substantially outperforming the one-component GP for detecting Earth-amplitude ictal events. Conclusions. Multi-component GP models that couple background neural variability with event characterisation are necessary for reliable detection of subtle ictal episodes in high-fidelity EEG recordings.
rewrites.math: Context. New photometric space missions to detect and characterise transiting exoplanets are focusing on bright stars to obtain high cadence, high signal-to-noise light curves. Since these missions will be sensitive to stellar oscillations and granulation even for dwarf stars, they will be limited by stellar variability. Robust methods to account for stellar variability are therefore crucial. Aims. We tested the performance of sparse Bayesian regression using relevance vector machines (RVMs) for the characterisation of transiting planets, determining how many basis functions are necessary to describe high cadence light curves expected from CHEOPS and PLATO. We selected bright stars observed in the CoRoT asteroseismology field at 32-second cadence. Methods. We modelled stellar variability by expanding it in a dictionary of physically motivated basis functions -- sinusoidal oscillation templates, exponential granulation kernels, and periodic rotation envelopes -- and applied the RVM objective to enforce automatic sparsity via type-II maximum likelihood over relevance weights. Model order selection followed marginal-likelihood comparison across candidate dictionaries. Results. The optimal sparse model retained four to five active basis vectors: one oscillation template, two to four granulation components, and one rotational modulation term. For Jupiter- and Neptune-size planets the sparse model matched or exceeded the full-basis fit; for Earth-size planets it recovered correct transit parameters whereas a single-component linear fit produced biased estimates. Conclusions. Sparse basis expansion via relevance vector machines, rather than Gaussian process covariance modelling, provides an effective and interpretable framework for disentangling stellar variability from planetary transit signals in high signal-to-noise TESS, CHEOPS, and PLATO light curves.

rewrites.reskin:
Matrix Completion Methods for Longitudinal Clinical Biomarker Imputation

In this paper we study methods for recovering missing biomarker measurements in longitudinal patient cohort studies, where clinical assessments are administered during some visits and the goal is imputing unobserved biomarker values for patient/visit combinations lacking measurement. We propose a class of matrix completion estimators that uses the observed entries of the patient-by-visit biomarker matrix corresponding to measured assessments to impute the missing entries corresponding to unassessed patient/visit combinations. This yields a matrix that well-approximates the original incomplete observation matrix while minimizing complexity according to the nuclear norm for matrices. We generalize results from the matrix completion literature by allowing the patterns of missing measurements to exhibit a temporal dependency structure arising from irregular admission schedules. We present novel insights concerning connections between the matrix completion literature, the literature on latent trajectory models, and the literatures on multiple imputation and covariate-adjusted outcome prediction. The proposed method outperforms mean-imputation or k-nearest-neighbor estimators in simulations based on real electronic health record data.
rewrites.math:
Factor-Augmented Regression Methods for Causal Panel Data Models

In this paper we study methods for estimating causal effects in settings with panel data, where some units are exposed to a treatment during some periods and the goal is estimating counterfactual outcomes for the treated unit/period combinations. We propose a class of interactive fixed effects estimators that extracts latent common factors from the control group outcome matrix using principal components regression, then projects treated unit pre-treatment outcomes onto those factors to construct synthetic counterfactuals. The estimated factors and loadings are obtained by iterating least-squares projections conditional on the factor structure, yielding an objective that minimizes the sum of squared residuals subject to a rank constraint imposed explicitly on the factor dimension rather than implicitly through a nuclear norm penalty. We allow the number of latent factors to be selected by cross-validation or information criteria. We present novel connections between the factor-augmented regression literature, the interactive fixed effects literature, and synthetic control methods. The proposed estimator outperforms unconfoundedness-based methods in simulations based on real data.

rewrites.reskin: We extend the classical mean-field (MF) energy minimization framework and propose a robust and sparse neuronal connectivity estimation model incorporating an ellipsoidal uncertainty set to reduce the impact of noisy calcium-imaging measurements and fixed wiring costs to penalize over-connectivity. In the literature, the MF model under fixed wiring costs is referred to as the sparse or cardinality-constrained MF optimization, a mixed integer problem that becomes intractable when the number of neurons is large. We develop an efficient semismooth Newton-based proximal difference-of-convex algorithm to solve the proposed model and prove its convergence to at least a local minimizer with a locally linear convergence rate. We explore properties of the robust and sparse connectivity graph both analytically and numerically. In particular, we show that MF optimization is a robust estimation procedure as long as the experimenter makes the proper choice on the regularization coefficient. We prove a one-to-one correspondence between this regularization coefficient and the level of robustness. Moreover, we characterize how the number of active synaptic connections changes with respect to the interaction between measurement uncertainty and the magnitude of wiring cost.
rewrites.math: We extend the classical mean-variance framework and propose a sparse portfolio selection model incorporating a Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) objective with an L1 regularization penalty to reduce sensitivity to tail-risk estimation errors and discourage excessive diversification. In the literature, L1-penalized CVaR minimization admits a linear programming reformulation, which scales tractably as the number of assets grows. We develop an efficient alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm to solve the proposed model and prove its convergence to the global minimizer with a sublinear convergence rate. We explore properties of the sparse CVaR-optimal portfolio both analytically and numerically. In particular, we show that CVaR minimization yields portfolios resilient to distributional misspecification as long as an investor makes the proper choice on the confidence level. We prove a one-to-one correspondence between the confidence level and portfolio sparsity. Moreover, we characterize how the number of held assets changes with respect to the interaction between tail-probability threshold and the magnitude of the L1 penalty.

rewrites.reskin:
Irregular sampling in neural spike trains and the use of the Lomb-Scargle periodogram

Detection of a periodic signal obscured by noise within a neural spike train is a central challenge in computational neuroscience, arising whenever electrode recordings contain contributions from oscillatory or semi-oscillatory neural rhythms driven by sensory stimulation, motor preparation, or intrinsic network dynamics. One of the most widely adopted frequency-domain tools for such analyses is the periodogram, yet its application to spike-train data is rarely straightforward. The optimal statistical properties of the classical periodogram are forfeited when action potentials are recorded on non-uniform temporal grids, a virtually universal condition in extracellular electrophysiology. The Lomb-Scargle (LS) technique recovers a portion of those properties, but at the cost of theoretical complications that obscure its interpretation and of implementations demanding bespoke software for computationally feasible execution. These drawbacks would be acceptable only if the LS periodogram materially outperformed simpler approximations. We demonstrate here that across a broad range of neural recording scenarios the simpler approaches yield estimates closely comparable to those of the LS periodogram. The interpretation of the effective Nyquist frequency under irregular spike-train sampling is also examined.
rewrites.math:
Irregular time series in astronomy and the use of Gaussian process regression for period estimation

Detection of a signal hidden by noise within a time series is an important problem in many astronomical searches, particularly for light curves exhibiting periodic or quasi-periodic variability due to rotating objects and other astrophysical phenomena. A principled alternative to periodogram-based approaches is Gaussian process (GP) regression, in which a covariance kernel with quasi-periodic structure is placed over the observational data and hyperparameters governing period, length-scale, and amplitude are inferred via marginal likelihood maximisation. Unlike spectral estimators, GP regression operates directly in the time domain, propagates photometric uncertainties through the posterior predictive distribution, and naturally accommodates irregular sampling without requiring any interpolation or reweighting scheme. However, the cubic computational cost of exact GP inference with respect to the number of observations poses scalability challenges for large surveys. In this work we compare GP period recovery against classical spectral techniques across a range of astrophysical time series, showing that GP regression provides calibrated uncertainty estimates alongside period detection. The analogue of the Nyquist limit in GP-based inference is also discussed.

rewrites.reskin:
A Hidden Markov Model for Rapidly Identifying Operational States from Manufacturing Process Streams

Electronic sensor arrays are frequently used to document machine behavior through time on industrial production lines. Methods that can identify underlying operational regimes driving specific process signatures can help engineers understand how and why equipment transitions between states, thereby aiding predictive maintenance and quality control. For sensor streams with significant measurement noise, a Bayesian state-space model analogous to the first-Difference Correlated Random Walk with Switching has often been applied. However, highly accurate sensor telemetry is now increasingly common in modern factories. We developed a Hidden Markov Movement Model for identifying operational states from process streams with negligible measurement error. We implemented as its basis the same process equation of the DCRWS, estimated via maximum likelihood using TMB for rapid fitting. We compared our model to a modified DCRWS for high-accuracy streams and to a common HMM fitted with moveHMM. The model proves accurate across multiple machine types by fitting it to real streams from a CNC lathe, an injection molder, and a conveyor system, as well as simulated data. It is made available through an R package.
rewrites.math:
A Particle Filter Approach for Rapidly Identifying Behavioral States from Animal Tracks

Electronic telemetry is frequently used to document animal movement through time. Methods that can identify underlying behaviors driving specific movement patterns help us understand how and why animals use available space, aiding conservation and management. For aquatic animal tracking data with significant measurement error, Bayesian state-space models have often been used. However, highly accurate tracking data are now becoming more common for aquatic species. We developed a sequential Monte Carlo (particle filter) method for identifying behavioral states from animal tracks with negligible error. Rather than the HMM's discrete latent-state emission model, our approach represents the behavioral state distribution as a weighted ensemble of particles propagated forward via importance resampling, with state assignments recovered by clustering particle trajectories. We compared this approach to the DCRWS NOME and to moveHMM on tracks from a grey seal, lake trout, and blue shark, as well as on simulated data. The particle filter handles multimodal state posteriors that maximum-likelihood HMM fitting cannot resolve and scales naturally to continuous behavioral gradients. It is available through the R package swim.

rewrites.reskin:
AnyScore/GPU: Accelerated Dynamic Programming for Real-Time Financial Risk Scoring on GPUs

The rapid expansion of high-frequency transaction streams in modern payment networks has driven demand for low-latency fraud detection at scale. Existing CPU-bound approaches cannot exploit the massively parallel architecture of contemporary GPUs, leaving substantial throughput headroom unused. We present AnyScore/GPU, a transaction risk-scoring library that adapts dynamic programming alignment to the domain of behavioral sequence matching against known fraud patterns. The approach minimizes global memory accesses through warp-shuffle communication between threads within a warp and employs half-precision arithmetic to double effective register throughput, achieving close-to-peak GPU utilization. Each transaction stream is treated as a sequence to be optimally aligned against a library of anomaly signatures, with the DP recurrence computing cumulative risk scores across state transitions. Benchmarks on synthetic payment datasets show throughput improvements of up to one order of magnitude over state-of-the-art CPU baselines, enabling real-time scoring of millions of transactions per second on a single GPU node.
rewrites.math:
AnySeq/BWT: Suffix-Array and FM-Index Search for High-Throughput Next-Generation Sequencing Alignment

The surge in reads produced by next-generation sequencing technologies demands alignment methods that scale beyond the quadratic cost of classical dynamic programming. We present AnySeq/BWT, a sequence alignment library that replaces the DP recurrence with FM-index traversal over a compressed Burrows-Wheeler Transform of the reference genome. Exact-match seed locations are identified in O(m) time via backward search, and candidate alignments are extended using a seed-and-extend chain model scored under an affine gap penalty. The BWT index is partitioned across GPU shared memory banks, and multiple query reads are processed concurrently through batched rank queries. Unlike warp-shuffle DP pipelines, the index-based approach eliminates the anti-diagonal wavefront dependency that limits GPU parallelism in classic alignment, allowing fully independent per-read scheduling. Experiments on human whole-genome short-read datasets demonstrate alignment throughput competitive with state-of-the-art tools while reducing peak memory bandwidth pressure relative to DP-based implementations.

rewrites.reskin: We introduce a fast Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) exploration of molecular force field parameter space using a modified version of the publicly available code FITMOL (Force field Iterative Tuning for MOLecules). The original FITMOL builds a grid of theoretical vibrational spectra from classical molecular dynamics simulations and fits to experimental infrared absorption measurements across wavenumber ranges from far-IR to near-IR to constrain parameters governing bond stretching, angle bending, and torsional potentials. Such a grid-based calibration can lead to prohibitively long parameter extraction because computation time grows exponentially with the number of force field terms considered, and results depend on sampling density fixed before each run. Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, by contrast, scale approximately linearly with the number of parameters, enabling faster and more accurate traversal of the force field parameter space through a smaller number of efficiently drawn samples. We test our MCMC implementation (called FITMOLMC) against simulated vibrational spectra. After verifying recovery of input force constants from synthetic data, we fit theoretical spectra to experimental measurements from the well-characterized NIST small-molecule benchmark set. We discuss parameter constraints and demonstrate the accuracy and CPU-time advantages of MCMC sampling over grid search.
rewrites.math: We introduce a variational Bayesian inference framework for galaxy parameter estimation using a mean-field approximate posterior within a modified version of the publicly available code CIGALE (Code Investigating GALaxy emission). The original CIGALE builds a grid of theoretical Spectral Energy Distribution (SED) models and fits to photometric fluxes from Ultraviolet (UV) to Infrared (IR) to constrain parameters related to galaxy formation and evolution. Rather than replacing the grid with Markov chain sampling, our approach optimizes the Evidence Lower BOund (ELBO) by iteratively updating a factored variational distribution over galaxy parameters, minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the approximate and true posteriors. This mean-field scheme avoids the sequential correlation inherent in chain-based methods and admits closed-form coordinate-ascent updates for conjugate parameter families, yielding deterministic convergence certificates absent in stochastic sampling. We test our variational version (CIGALEVI) on simulated photometric data, verifying parameter recovery from mock SEDs, and subsequently apply it to real photometry from the SINGS sample. We discuss posterior approximation quality, compare uncertainty estimates against analytic benchmarks, and demonstrate improvements in computational efficiency over grid-based methods.

MECHANISM: Given an ensemble of noisy profile measurements of a target entity, each measurement is assumed to arise from a mixture of offset positions around an approximate location. The offset is parameterized by a two-parameter model (e.g., mean and spread). For each measurement, a likelihood is computed by integrating or summing the contribution of each offset component weighted by mixture probabilities. Parameters are estimated by maximizing the joint likelihood across measurements.
DOMAIN: Astronomy, cosmology, observational measurement.

DATA_OBJECT: dense matrix or tensor
INFERENCE: maximum likelihood
PROBLEM_FORM: estimation
DISTRIBUTION: observed; Gaussian mixture

Extract a single dominant factor and use the loading of each entity onto that factor as a scalar importance score. Compare the distribution of these scores across entities to reference distributions, and examine whether the leading factor exhibits particular structural properties in its loadings.

The posterior predictive distribution quantifies uncertainty in period estimates and naturally accommodates non-uniform sampling. Computational scaling is cubic in observation count.
